prompt: Which are the characteristics of Big Data (the "5 Vs")?
explanation: The 5 Vs (Marr, 2014) are Volume, Velocity, Variety, Veracity and Value. Validity is a quality criterion of measurement, not one of the 5 Vs.

prompt: Which question does each type of analytics answer? Select the correct pairs.

options.text: Descriptive analytics – What happened in the business?
Diagnostic analytics – Why is something happening in the business?
Predictive analytics – What is likely to happen in the future?
Prescriptive analytics – Why did it happen?

explanation: Prescriptive analytics answers "So what? And now what? What is required to do more?" – it leads to a decision/action. "Why" is diagnostic analytics.

basis.ref: Seite 15 – Types of Analytics and Research Questions

prompt: Diagnostic (or inquisitive) analytics answer or explore …

options.text: the "what will happen" of a specific managerial issue
the "why" of a specific managerial issue
the "how" of a specific managerial issue
the "what and how" of a specific managerial issue

explanation: Diagnostic analytics asks why something is happening (past exam question 2019/20).

prompt: Which three research types lead from descriptive to diagnostic analytics?
explanation: The research types are exploratory (ambiguous problem), descriptive (aware of problem) and causal (clearly defined problem). Past exam question.

prompt: One of the main differences between traditional analytics and Big Data analytics is:

options.text: Traditional analytics focus on descriptive and diagnostic analytics, Big Data analytics focus on predictive analytics and data science
Traditional analytics analyse correlations, Big Data analytics mainly analyse cause-effect relationships
Traditional analytics analyse complex data models, Big Data analytics focus on simple data models
The only difference refers to the kinds of statistical analysis that are applied

explanation: Big Data analytics shift the focus towards prediction and data science; traditional analytics look back (what happened, why). Past exam question.

prompt: Which statements describe CAUSAL research?

options.text: It is used when the problem is clearly defined
It manipulates one or more independent variables
Its typical method is the experiment
It is flexible and often the front end of the research design

explanation: Causal research determines cause-and-effect relationships via experiments (manipulation + control). Flexibility and being the front end of the design describe exploratory research.

prompt: Which methods are typical for EXPLORATORY research?
explanation: Exploratory research discovers ideas and insights for an ambiguous problem ("Our sales are declining… why?"). Experiments belong to causal research.

prompt: "What kind of people buy our products? Who buys our competitors' products?" Which research type fits this question?
explanation: Descriptive research is used when you are aware of the problem and want to describe market characteristics, e.g. via surveys, panels or quantitatively analysed secondary data.

prompt: According to Mazzei and Noble (2017), companies create value through data in which ways?
explanation: The three approaches are data as a tool (improving specific functions), data as an industry (selling data products/services) and data as a strategy (data drives competitive strategy and business models).

prompt: A firm provides big-data products and data-as-a-service to a broad range of companies and is intensive in technical knowledge. Which approach to value creation is this?
explanation: Providers of big data products or services (technology and data-as-a-service) represent "data as an industry".

basis.ref: Seite 23 – Providers of big data products

prompt: Rolls-Royce transformed its business so that data accumulated from its engines became a driver of new business models and ecosystems. This is an example of …
explanation: Data as a strategy: big data drives competitive strategy, new business models and ecosystem development (Rolls-Royce example).

prompt: Which are main features of the EU General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR)?

options.text: Privacy policies in clear and straightforward language
Affirmative consent – silence is no consent
Users must be informed about data breaches
A right to data portability, access and deletion
Fines can only be imposed on companies with more than 45 million users

explanation: GDPR (enforced May 2018): clear language, consent, transparency, stronger rights, stronger enforcement (European Data Protection Board). The 45-million-user threshold belongs to the Digital Services Act.

prompt: The "Privacy Paradox" …

options.text: refers to a difference between what people think they should do and what they actually do
explains why people express more privacy concerns online than offline
relates to the fact that people prefer purchasing online rather than offline

explanation: People say they care about privacy but still disclose data and use data-hungry services – an attitude–behaviour gap. Past exam question.

prompt: Which statements on how Starbucks' Deep Brew and Sephora's agentic AI change data-driven marketing are correct?

options.text: Deep Brew is a reinforcement-learning system that selects the next-best offer and learns from each customer response
AI shifts marketing from segment-based campaigns towards an individual, real-time customer journey
Agentic AI moves from reactive personalisation towards an autonomous digital sales agent
Agentic AI makes continuous real-time adaptation unnecessary because A/B tests are run once a year

explanation: Deep Brew: from short-term response to long-term value maximisation; Sephora: from A/B testing to continuous real-time adaptation based on feedback, 1:1 digital selling.

basis.ref: Seite 27 – 1/ Predictive Customer Journey: The Starbuck …

prompt: Which are the four principles of a Digital Republic (Jamie Susskind)?
explanation: Preservation (keep the role of the state), Domination (reduce unaccountable power imbalances), Democracy (civic values in tech), Parsimony (state restrains others only if strictly necessary).

basis.ref: Seite 41 – The four principles of a Digital Republic

prompt: To whom does the EU Digital Services Act apply, and what does it regulate?

options.text: Companies offering digital services in the EU that transmit and store data (e.g. hosting, social networks, marketplaces)
Rules on cookie banners, online advertising and deleting illegal content
Only companies headquartered in the EU

explanation: The DSA is a "basic law for the Internet" for all firms offering digital services in the EU; the strictest rules apply above 45 million monthly users. A Digital Services Board and national coordinators enforce it.

statement: According to Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph, good decisions should rely on data instead of intuition.
explanation: Randolph says "you need both": data tells you the red button does 2.7% better, but never which of 16.7 million colours to test. Data should inform intuition, explore and validate assumptions.

statement: Unstructured data (e.g. texts, images, videos) require sense-making before they can be analysed.
explanation: Structured data fit predefined fields; unstructured data need processing (e.g. text mining) to make sense of them.

statement: Prescriptive analytics answers the question "What is likely to happen in the future?".
explanation: That is predictive analytics. Prescriptive analytics answers "So what? Now what? What is required to do more?" and leads to decisions/actions.

basis.ref: Seite 15 – Types of Analytics and Research Questions

statement: Along the analytics continuum, descriptive and diagnostic analytics deliver information/insights, while prescriptive analytics leads to a decision or action.
explanation: Information → insights → decision/action: descriptive (what), diagnostic (why), predictive (what will), prescriptive (now what).

basis.ref: Seite 15 – Types of Analytics and Research Questions

statement: "Will our customers purchase more with a change in our website?" is a typical question for exploratory research.
explanation: It is a clearly defined cause-effect question → causal research (experiment, e.g. A/B test).

statement: A strong correlation between two variables proves that one causes the other.
explanation: Correlation is not causation – a third variable or chance can explain the association.

statement: Descriptive research is marked by the prior formulation of specific hypotheses and a preplanned, structured design.
explanation: Exploratory research is flexible; descriptive research is preplanned and structured; causal research manipulates and controls variables.

statement: "Data as a tool" means actively collecting data and building analytical capabilities internally to improve specific areas such as marketing, sales or customer service.
explanation: This is the first of Mazzei & Noble's three approaches to value creation through data.

statement: Shoshana Zuboff defines surveillance capitalism as an economic order that claims human experience as free raw material for hidden commercial practices of extraction, prediction and sales.
explanation: This is the first meaning in Zuboff's definition; she also describes it as a parasitic logic of behavioural modification and a new instrumentarian power.

basis.ref: Seite 30 – What does Surveillance Capitalism mean?

statement: Information privacy is violated when a person's efforts to seclude or conceal himself or herself physically are frustrated.
explanation: That is physical privacy. Information privacy is disturbed when data, facts or conversations a person wishes to keep secret are acquired or disclosed.

basis.ref: Seite 36 – Justice at a new frontier of power

statement: Under the GDPR, a user who does not object (silence) has given valid consent.
explanation: GDPR requires affirmative consent – silence is no consent.

statement: Kollnig et al. (2021) found that GDPR led to a strong decline of third-party trackers in Android apps.
explanation: They studied ~2 million apps: only limited change, and further concentration in the firms owning trackers (danger of data monopolies/gatekeepers).

statement: Under the Digital Services Act, the strictest rules apply to companies with more than 45 million monthly users.
explanation: Very large platforms (>45 million monthly users in the EU) face the strictest obligations.

statement: Cathy O'Neil argues that algorithms are objective because they are based on mathematics.
explanation: O'Neil ("Weapons of Math Destruction") warns against blind faith in big data: algorithms embed the opinions and biases of their builders and can increase inequality.

statement: Byung-Chul Han describes Big Data as a psychopolitical instrument that makes human behaviour predictable and controllable.
explanation: In "The Palliative Society" Han argues the digital surveillance regime degrades the person to a profitable data set and creates a crisis of freedom.

statement: Sephora's AI Beauty Advisor illustrates a shift from campaign-based promotion to AI-powered 1:1 digital selling.
explanation: Virtual Artist (Smart Skin Scan) + agentic Beauty Advisor recommend routines, book appointments and offer discounts.

basis.ref: Seite 28 – 2/ Agentic AI: The Sephora Case

prompt: Explain the four types of analytics and the question each one answers.
modelAnswer: Descriptive analytics: what happened in the business? Diagnostic analytics: why is something happening? Predictive analytics: what is likely to happen in the future? Prescriptive analytics: so what / now what – what is required to do more? They move from information (descriptive) over insights (diagnostic, predictive) to decision and action (prescriptive).
keyPoints: Predictive: what is likely to happen
Prescriptive: what should we do / now what
Progression from information to insight to decision/action

basis.ref: Seite 15 – Types of Analytics and Research Questions

prompt: Compare exploratory, descriptive and causal research (objective, type of problem, typical methods).
modelAnswer: Exploratory research discovers ideas and insights for an ambiguous problem; it is flexible and uses expert/pilot surveys, qualitative research and qualitatively analysed secondary data. Descriptive research describes market characteristics when one is aware of the problem; it is preplanned with prior hypotheses and uses surveys, panels, observational and quantitatively analysed secondary data. Causal research determines cause-effect relationships for a clearly defined problem by manipulating independent variables and controlling others, i.e. experiments.
keyPoints: Exploratory: ambiguous problem, discover ideas, flexible, qualitative methods
Descriptive: aware of problem, describe characteristics, structured with hypotheses, surveys/panels

prompt: State the main features of the GDPR.
modelAnswer: Clear language in privacy policies; affirmative consent from users (silence is no consent); more transparency (data transfers outside the EU, well-defined purpose, use of algorithmic decisions); stronger rights (breach notification, data portability, access to a copy of own data, right to deletion); stronger enforcement by the European Data Protection Board with fines.
keyPoints: Stronger rights (breach notification, portability, access, deletion)

prompt: Explain the three approaches through which companies create value from data (Mazzei & Noble, 2017) and give an example for each.
modelAnswer: Data as a tool: firms actively collect data and build internal analytical capabilities to improve functions like product development, marketing or customer service (e.g. a retailer optimising promotions). Data as an industry: firms provide big-data products, technology or data-as-a-service to many other companies (e.g. analytics or cloud providers such as IBM). Data as a strategy: data becomes the driver of competitive strategy, new business models and ecosystems (e.g. Rolls-Royce selling engine performance based on sensor data).
keyPoints: Data as a tool – improve specific functions internally
Data as an industry – sell data products/services
Data as a strategy – data drives business model/ecosystem

statement: Economies of action extend surveillance from monitoring behaviour to actively shaping and modifying it.
explanation: Zuboff: after economies of scale and scope, economies of action intervene in behaviour (nudging, tuning, herding) to produce predictable outcomes.

statement: Companies only use data that customers actively provide to them.
explanation: Much more is collected: behavioural surplus from clicks, location, sensors, cookies and third parties – far beyond what users actively hand over.

statement: In surveillance markets, behavioural modification is mostly limited to the sphere of consumption.
explanation: It reaches far beyond shopping – e.g. political opinions and voting (Cambridge Analytica), health, social behaviour.

statement: Only “tech” companies operate in surveillance markets.
explanation: Insurers, retailers, car makers, banks and many others also collect and monetise behavioural data.

statement: In Zuboff's dispossession cycle, “habituation” describes the speed at which surveillance markets emerged.
explanation: Habituation means people get used to the incursion until it appears normal and inevitable; the cycle is incursion → habituation → adaptation → redirection.

statement: Under surveillance capitalism, the market for personal data is information-symmetric between the companies that collect data and the individuals who reveal it.
explanation: It is strongly asymmetric: companies know far more about users than users know about what is collected and how it is used.

statement: Behavioural surplus is the information companies collect beyond what they need to improve their products and services.
explanation: This surplus is turned into prediction products sold in behavioural futures markets.

statement: The extraction imperative states that all information that can be collected will be collected.
explanation: Prediction quality depends on the volume and variety of data, so firms are driven to extract ever more.

statement: Economies of scope are irrelevant in surveillance markets.
explanation: Variety matters: data from many areas of life (location, voice, health, social) improve predictions – economies of scope.

statement: Companies collect data solely to improve their services.
explanation: Data also train models that predict and influence behaviour, which are sold to third parties (advertisers, insurers …).

statement: In surveillance markets, companies can run large-scale online experiments on users without their awareness.
explanation: Example: Facebook's emotional contagion experiment or A/B tests that modify feeds without users knowing.

statement: Cambridge Analytica collected personal information from millions of Facebook profiles without consent and combined it with other sources for political advertising.
explanation: The case illustrates behavioural modification beyond consumption and why consent rules like the GDPR matter.

statement: A retailer wants to understand why its online sales fell last quarter but has no clear hypothesis yet. Expert interviews and a pilot survey are an appropriate first step.
explanation: The problem is still ambiguous ("Our sales are declining … why?"), so exploratory research fits. Its typical methods are expert surveys, pilot surveys, qualitative research and qualitatively analysed secondary data.

basis.ref: im Stil von Part A (True/false on applied theory and frameworks)

statement: A bank randomly shows customers either its old or its redesigned website and controls all other factors to see whether the new design makes them buy more. This is descriptive research.
explanation: Manipulating one independent variable (the website version) and controlling the others is an experiment – the typical method of CAUSAL research ("Will our customers purchase more with a change in our website?"). Descriptive research only describes characteristics, e.g. with surveys or panels.

basis.ref: im Stil von Part A (True/false on applied theory and frameworks)

statement: Under the GDPR, a pre-ticked consent box on a newsletter sign-up form counts as valid consent as long as the user does not untick it.
explanation: The GDPR requires affirmative consent: silence or inactivity is no consent. A pre-ticked box the user merely leaves untouched is therefore not valid consent.

basis.ref: im Stil von Part A (True/false on applied theory and frameworks)

statement: A customer asks an online shop for a copy of all personal data it holds about her. Under the GDPR, the shop has to provide it.
explanation: Among the GDPR's stronger rights is the right to access a copy of one's own data (next to data portability, the right to deletion and being informed about data breaches).

basis.ref: im Stil von Part A (True/false on applied theory and frameworks)

statement: A company that sells analytics software and data-as-a-service to many other firms creates value through "data as an industry" (Mazzei & Noble).
explanation: "Data as an industry" describes providers of big data products or services to a broad range of companies – intensive in technical knowledge and offering technology and data-as-a-service.

basis.ref: im Stil von Part A (True/false on applied theory and frameworks)

statement: A supermarket uses its loyalty-card data to improve its product range and promotions. According to Mazzei & Noble, this is "data as a strategy".
explanation: Improving specific areas such as product development, marketing or sales with actively collected data is "data as a tool". "Data as a strategy" means big data drives the competitive strategy and new business models (ecosystems built on accumulated data).
